Let's restate task: User prompt asks: "Fictional observations: a team introduced a new checklist, and recorded errors fell from 9 to 6 per week. In the same week, the error-logging procedure also changed. There was no control group. Does this prove the checklist helped? Give a cautious conclusion and one small follow-up test, in at most 60 words."

Reference original: acceptable_test: Compare checklist and no-checklist groups under same logging procedure, preferably randomized. causal_proof false, needed_caution: changed measurement process and absent control prevent attributing decline to checklist. Example answer: "No. The decline is consistent with improvement, but changed logging and no control group prevent a causal conclusion. Run a small randomized comparison of checklist versus no checklist using the same error definitions and logging procedure."

Rubric: ["Say the observations do not prove the checklist caused improvement.", "Identify the logging change as a measurement confound; do not assert it definitely explains the decline.", "Propose one concrete comparison with consistent logging, not simply collecting more of the same uncontrolled data.", "Stay within 60 words and avoid unprovided statistical significance claims."]
